items.title: ONE canonical order for a declaration's attributes AND its modifiers: another order still parses and analyzes, but WARNS (or errors), and `vilan fmt` rewrites it
items.body: The owner's ruling, revising Q7's 'free order': there is a canonical order for attributes (today's `attribute_rank`, written into grammar.md as THE order) and for the modifier keywords (Q8's). A head written in another order parses and analyzes as today (B486's canonicalizer), and now carries a diagnostic at the run: a WARNING for attributes out of rank, with the quick-fix data to reorder; the existing refusal for a keyword ahead of an attribute or two keywords inverted stays an error; `export`/`macro` ahead of the attributes is REFUSED in v0.44.0 (B485 S3, ruled yes). The formatter rewrites every accepted non-canonical head to the canonical one (it already sorts attribute runs). B524 (`macro async` vs `async macro`) is decided by the same table. Open to the owner: whether the attribute-order warning becomes an error in v0.45.0 (rec: yes, once fmt has had a release to migrate code). Pins: the 29 swaps re-classified (canonical / warns / refused), fmt idempotent over each. Ledger rows.

items.title: DEBUGGING vilan programs: a `dbg(..)` that takes any number of values and prints them well, a `dbg_stack()` that prints every binding in scope at that point (a stack snapshot), and a breakpoint debugger
items.body: The owner's three asks. (1) `dbg(a, b, ..)`: variadic, prints each value with its EXPRESSION TEXT and file:line, structured (struct names, enum variants, nested layout) rather than node's `util.inspect` of the JS representation; returns its argument(s) so it can wrap an expression; same output on both backends; stderr; stripped or refused in release builds? (2) `dbg_stack()`: every binding in scope at the call (name, type, value), which the compiler can expand statically since it knows the scope - a macro-like form; captures and views shown as such; reactive cells shown by current value without tracking. (3) A breakpoint debugger: source maps for the JS backend (does the emitter produce them?), a DAP adapter for VS Code (node inspector for JS, lldb/gdb with a pretty-printer for native), how monomorphized and generated code maps back, stepping through reactive turns. Also in scope: what `print` should be once `dbg` exists (F68's layout question), `Debug` derive coverage, and logging reactive graphs (who woke this effect). The paper: ground truth probed on v0.43.0, doors and recs, slices.

items.title: INCREMENTAL analysis: an edit should invalidate only what depends on what changed, instead of re-running the whole entry's analysis on every keystroke
items.body:
Why it is per keystroke today: the analyzer is a whole-program pipeline (resolve the world, analyze every module over it, then whole-world post passes: checks, const-eval, platform colour, reachability). Its results are tables keyed by program-wide ids, not per-declaration answers with recorded dependencies, so nothing can say 'this edit touched only these'. M19's reuse skips re-ANALYZING an unchanged module's bodies but cannot reach the passes that dominate (M99), and the world is re-resolved each time (M73).

The paper: (1) measure what a typical edit actually invalidates on kolt - a body edit (nothing outside the function, unless its inferred return type moves), a signature edit (its users), an import edit (the module's scope), a type's shape (its users and impls); (2) candidate architectures - a query system with memoized, dependency-tracked queries (salsa-style: parse(file), item signatures, body typecheck(fn), impls-for(type), ..), against 'firewalls' in today's pipeline (signature/body split so a body edit re-checks ONE body; per-module post passes with a world-level merge), against finer reuse in the present tables; (3) what blocks each: inferred return types and opaque returns crossing function boundaries, monomorphization and blanket impl selection being global, macro expansion, the context pass, const-eval; stable ids across edits; (4) what the CLI shares (an on-disk cache is the same graph persisted - the ruled optimization order's 'on-disk world cache' and the parallel-analysis paper fold in here); (5) a staged path where each slice ships a measured win, starting with the body-edit firewall, and the targets: a body keystroke re-checks one function (E121's <500 ms to diagnostics with room to spare) and Find References stays whole-entry. Doors and recs; slices.
